label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
# Glenmore, and what happens next

I'm writing this once, to all of you together, because some of you have already heard pieces of it from someone else, and that isn't how I wanted you to find out. That's my fault, and I'm sorry for it. I'll say more about that further down.

So here it is, plainly. The house at Glenmore, near Oughterard, is sold. The sale was agreed on 3 November and it closes on 15 January 2027.

Most of you know the house as the Mulkerrin place, or as the place where Dad grew up, or as the one with the haggard out the back and the lake below it. Pádraig Mulkerrin, Tom's grandfather, built it in 1931. Tom was born there and he came back to it all his life, even after we moved to town. He died in March 2024. Since then I've been driving out there every second week, forty minutes each way, to air the place and run the taps and check the pipes and sit in the kitchen for a while. I kept telling myself that I'd decide about it when I was ready. I wasn't ready. But I've stopped pretending that being ready was ever going to come on its own.

## Who's buying it

Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, so some of you may know the family already. They have two small children and they want to live in the house. They are not buying it as a holiday let, and they are not buying it to flip it. I asked them that straight out, because I'd have been a fool not to, and they didn't flinch. Aoife told me the first time they walked through the front door that the kitchen was where she wanted to be. I won't pretend that didn't affect me.

I had other offers. In the summer a couple of people from Dublin came out, and one of them offered more than the Joyces did. I took the lower offer on purpose. I want to be clear about that because some of you will hear "lower" and think I was careless or soft. I wasn't. The price I accepted is fair, and I could have asked for more. But I wanted the house to go to people who would live in it and bring children into it, which is what Tom always wanted. He used to say the house should have children in it, not be a museum. I didn't want it to become a holiday home with the lights off for eleven months of the year. The Joyces want the lights on. That was the deciding thing for me.

## Why I'm selling

Some of you will ask why I'm selling at all, so I'll tell you the reasons, and I'll tell you the uncomfortable ones too.

The first is money, and it isn't a small matter. In September I had the roof surveyed by Ó Flaithearta's. The slates need doing and the back chimney needs rebuilding. The quote came to €38,000, and that doesn't include the damp in the back bedroom, which is a problem in itself and which nobody can tell me the full cost of until they open the wall. And the septic tank needs replacing. That would have had to be done before anyone could sell the house to anyone, so it wasn't something I could skip. I had a choice between spending money I don't have on a house I can't live in, or selling it to people who can. I know that sounds like an estate agent talking, and I didn't want it to sound like that, but it's the truth.

The second reason is harder to write down. Since the autumn, I've been frightened to be out there on my own. I don't mean I'm frightened of the house. I mean I'm frightened of what happens if something goes wrong, and nobody knows I'm there.

That brings me to something I haven't told anyone. Last February I slipped on the step at the back door. There was frost on it and I went down hard. I lay on the step for twenty minutes before I could get up. Nobody was near. My phone was in the car, which was not where I needed it to be. I got myself up in the end and drove home very carefully and sat in the kitchen in town until my hands stopped shaking. I didn't tell anyone, not even the girls. I should have. I'm telling you now because it's part of why I can't keep going the way I have been, and because I don't want to hide it anymore.

The third reason, and the one that took me the longest, is this: over the best part of two years I've come to understand that I can keep Tom's memory without keeping the house. I used to think the two were the same thing. They aren't. Tom is in the dresser, in the fiddle, in the photographs, in the way he said "grand" as if it were a complete sentence. He is not in the walls. I'd have kept the walls if I could have, but I can't, and I don't think he'd want me to fall on a step for them.

## What's being kept

I want you to know exactly what's coming with me, because I think you need to see the list rather than take my word for it.

The dresser is going to Úna. It's been in the front room since before any of us were born, and it's too big for anywhere I'm going to live. Úna, you'll have to find a wall for it. I'm sorry about the stairs, I'm told it doesn't go up them.

Pádraig's fiddle is coming with me. Some of you have asked about it already. I haven't decided yet whether it goes to Declan or to one of the grandchildren, and I'd rather not decide that on my own. I'll put it to the family once we've all had the chance to talk.

The photographs are all coming with me, every one. I've been through the boxes and I've made copies of the ones I think nobody else has. If you want a copy of anything specific, write to me and I'll send it.

The Sacred Heart lamp is coming. It's been plugged in beside the back door since the sixties and I don't think it's ever been switched off properly. The gate sign is coming too. Declan, you'll remember it. You painted the letters when you were twelve and you got the "G" wrong, and Dad never let anybody fix it.

And the Joyces have said that family can come out and walk the land whenever we like. I've asked them, and they've meant it. The haggard, the lake, the path down past the old well, all of it. That's a gift and I'm grateful for it, and I'd like you to know it wasn't something I had to beg for.

## How you found out

This is the part I'm most ashamed of.

Some of you heard about the sale before I'd told you properly. I didn't mean that to happen, but it did, and the fault is mine. I should have sat everyone down, or rung each of you, before a single word went out. Instead I let it drift, and by the time I got around to saying it, you'd heard it from someone else, and it looked like I'd been hiding it. I wasn't exactly hiding it. But I didn't do the decent thing, and I know that now.

Declan heard it from his cousin Gráinne on a WhatsApp message. He rang me at two in the morning, his time, and he was in pieces. He said I was "selling Dad." I said things back to him that I shouldn't have said. I won't repeat them here, and I'm not going to excuse them either. He was hurt and I answered his hurt with my own, and that was wrong of me. I'm sorry, Declan. You deserved to hear it from me, first and properly, and you didn't.

I'm sorry for how you all found out. I'm not sorry for the decision. I know those two things look like they should go together, but I'm not going to pretend I'm sorry I sold the house when I'm not. I am sorry I didn't tell you the right way, and I regret not talking it through with Declan before it was agreed. He has every right to be upset about that, and I'd have done it differently if I could.

I also know I'm asking you to accept the decision now, when it's already made. I'm not going to wait until Declan's summer visit to close it, because the Joyces need to know where they stand and the solicitors need a date, and because if I wait for everyone to be comfortable, I'll be at that back step again in February with nobody to hear me. That's the honest reason. It isn't a good enough reason to make you feel better, but it's the one I've got.

## For Declan

I want to say something directly to you, Declan, because I know you'll read this, and I know you'll read it more than once.

I'm not angry with you. I was angry at the phone call, and I shouldn't have been, because you were grieving and you had every reason to be. Whatever you said that night, I've had time to think, and I understand it. You loved that place. You grew up in it. You were the one who swam out to the rock and wouldn't come out of the lake until your lips were blue, and I stood on the bank shouting at you and you wouldn't listen to a word. I think about that a lot. You were stubborn about the lake and you were stubborn about Dad, and I don't blame you for either.

The door is open. It's always been open. If you want to come out to Glenmore before the 15th, to walk the land or to sit in the kitchen or just to stand in the haggard where Dad proposed to me in the rain in 1979 with the cattle watching us, you're welcome, any time. If you want to talk on the phone at a reasonable hour, I'll pick up. If you want to be angry for a while longer, that's all right too. I'd rather have you angry and talking to me than quiet and gone.

## Please come to the day out

On Sunday 13 December, before the house is cleared, we're having a family day out at Glenmore. I'm asking everyone who can to come. Whether you're in Boston or Perth or Leeds or just up the road, if you can get there, please do. We'll have soup and sandwiches and tea in the big pot, and there'll be a fire going in the front room for as long as the chimney allows. Bring wellies, because the path down to the lake is a disgrace in December and it has been for as long as I can remember.

If you can't make it, I understand. Christmas is a hard enough time to travel. But if you can, I'd like to see you. I'd like us to walk the land together one more time as a family, and to tell the stories while they're still in the rooms.

The Joyces have said they'll be there for the afternoon, and I'd like you to meet them. They're decent people. They're not the enemy, and they're not the Dublin crowd. They're a young couple with two small children who want to make a home in a house that's been a home for ninety years. I'd like to think Pádraig would have liked them too.

## Last things

I've spent a lot of this post explaining, and I'm not sure it's all in the right order, so let me finish simply.

Tom and I had forty-five years in that house, on and off. We had the best summers of our lives out there and some of the worst winters. We raised three children there. We buried a lot of our own people from it. We were happy there, and I don't want anyone to read this and think otherwise. I'm grateful for every one of those years.

I'm also a woman of seventy-one who has had a bad fall on a frozen step and was lucky to get back up. I'm a retired teacher who can add up a roof quote and a septic tank and know what they come to. And I'm someone who has, at last, understood that love doesn't always mean holding on to the building. Sometimes it means letting the place go to people who will make it live again, and carrying the people and the stories with you.

I'll tell you the date again so nobody has to hear it from someone else: the sale closes on 15 January 2027. Between now and then there'll be a lot of boxes, a lot of phone calls, and I expect a few more tears. But there'll also be the 13th of December, and soup, and wellies, and everyone in the one room for an afternoon.

Please come if you can. Please ring me if you need to. And please know that I'm sorry for how this reached you, and that I love every one of you more than I can say in a blog post.

Love to you all,
Mam
